name: Fordata
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_quote: In Fordata stress always falls on the penultimate syllable. Long vowels are disyllabic, when they occur in final position stress falls on the first part, giving the appearance of final stress. Stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable in nouns of which the root ends in a consonant when they are followed by a possessive suffix singular. When a noun ends in a 2nd or 3rd person plural possessive …

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in the held Drabbe 1926 scanned at the stated pages. The best available source (Marshall 2000, PL-503:197-199, section 4 'Stress') is held and read here; it independently confirms fixed penultimate stress on the phonological word, stress not contrastive, prefixes irrelevant, monosyllabic enclitics (pl. ra, particle a, genitive -n/-m/-ng after r-final roots) extrametrical, disyllabic genitive enclitics (-rira, -bira, -dida, -mami) shifting stress to the new penult. Nothing contradicts the fixed-strict penult coding. Action: fill the empty cite/quote/loc/grade fields with Marshall 2000 p.197-198 as the deciding citation (Drabbe 1926:6-7 as corroborating older primary), and optionally note the enclitic extrametricality in the rule notes.

sources.quote: p. 6: "In Fordata the stress always falls on the penultimate syllable. One should not forget, however, that two adjacent vowels form two syllables, as e.g. in akaa 'what', so the stress falls on the a right after the k — seemingly the final syllable." p. 7: "In one single case the stress is on the antepenultimate syllable, namely in relational nouns whose root ends in a consonant, when they take a possessive suffix of the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd person singular, e.g. soemar 'mouth', soemaran 'his mouth
